newsitem.title: ITALY: U.N. agency warns 80,000 children may die in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: U.N. agency warns 80,000 children may die in Zaire.

text.p: More than 80,000 children under the age of three will die in eastern Zaire by the end of the month unless humanitarian aid corridors are opened to starving refugees, the head of the U.N.'s food aid agency said on Friday.

"People are already starting to die and we estimate that by the end of the month over 80,000 children under three will die," Catherine Bertini, executive director of the World Food Programme (WFP), told Reuters in an interview.

"They'll die because of the lack of food, the lack of sanitation and the lack of water and of the diseases that have quickly moved through those populations," the American head of the Rome-based agency said.
"There are over a million people wandering around or hiding with not only no access to food but no access to water or sanitation," she said.
Bertini, who warned of a spreading humanitarian crisis as a result of the fighting in the region, spoke in an interview ahead of next week's World Food Summit in Rome.

She said there was an "absolute, immediate need for humanitarian corridors to be opened and for us to be able to move food through, for people to be able to move water and medical supplies and international staff through," she said.
Bertini called for "some sort of ceasefire" to allow aid workers to move in.
WFP has enough food in the Great Lakes Region to feed people until the end of January but cannot get it through.
"Military intervention is one solution but the local governments could also agree to allow this to happen and those political agreements are not yet in place," Bertini said.
"It's a tragic situation and political solutions are the only solutions and we must have them otherwise we cannot physically move in and save lives," she said.
Rwanda has said it is opposed to French participation in a U.N. humanitarian force to open aid corridors for over a million Rwandan and Burundian refugees trapped in the fighting.
Bertini spoke as aid workers in Goma, Zaire, said war was affecting an increasingly wide area, with more people fleeing and ever greater numbers going hungry.

"If the crisis in eastern Zaire is not solved soon it could spill over all throughout the region even more than it already has," she said. "This could spread depending on which way people flee and where the insecurity grows."
Bertini said that the WFP had prepositioned food in Rwanda to give to refugees who eventually choose to return.
"We will give it to every refugee coming back home so that they can take it and use it while they get resettled back home," she said.
The Zaire crisis has thrown a sharp and immediate focus on next week's World Food Summit, organised by the U.N.'s Food and Agriculture Organisation which is also Rome-based.
The summit will commit leaders to reducing the number of undernourished people to half their present level of 840 million by no later than 2015.
"The World Food Summit will have been effective if after it's over leaders go home and actually implement the proposals in the plan," Bertini said.

"What needs to happen in the long term is that donor countries need to put food aid higher on their priority list and we need to convince their populations, their taxpayers, their voters, that it is in their interest to do this."
